claim: P. pacificus and C. elegans diverged an estimated 60–90 million years ago.
source: Although C. elegans and P. pacificus diverged an estimated 60–90 million years ago (Werner et al., 2018), they share the same number of chromosomes (2n = 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Werner et al., 2018.

claim: P. pacificus and C. elegans share the same number of chromosomes (2n = 12).
source: Although C. elegans and P. pacificus diverged an estimated 60–90 million years ago (Werner et al., 2018), they share the same number of chromosomes (2n = 12).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about these species.

claim: Macrosynteny is largely maintained between P. pacificus and C. elegans, other than one major chromosomal translocation.
source: Other than one major chromosomal translocation, macrosynteny is largely maintained between the two species (Dieterich et al., 2008; Rödelsperger et al., 2017) as well as other Rhabditids.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dieterich et al., 2008 and Rödelsperger et al., 2017.

claim: P. pacificus has holocentric chromosomes.
source: Like other nematodes, P. pacificus is thought to have holocentric chromosomes, which we confirm here through cytological analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by cytological analysis presented in the manuscript, specifically the distribution of CENP-C on mitotic chromosomes shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The distribution of CENP-C on mitotic chromosomes in P. pacificus confirmed their holocentric organization.
source: The distribution of CENP-C on mitotic chromosomes in embryos and mitotic germ cells confirmed their holocentric organization (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing CENP-C distribution in Figure 1D.

claim: Kinetochores in P. pacificus appeared as linear structures along the full length of each chromatid on mitotic chromosomes, rather than discrete foci.
source: Kinetochores appeared as linear structures along the full length of each chromatid on mitotic chromosomes, rather than discrete foci.
evidence: This observation is based on CENP-C immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CENP-C coated the chromosomes during meiotic metaphase I in P. pacificus.
source: CENP-C also coated the chromosomes during meiotic metaphase I (Figure 1C), as in C. elegans (Shakes et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1C and comparison to C. elegans data from Shakes et al., 2009.

claim: The P. pacificus genome contains an open-reading frame encoding an unambiguous ortholog of Dmc1.
source: BLAST searches of the P. pacificus genome revealed an open-reading frame encoding an unambiguous ortholog of Dmc1, a meiosis-specific paralog of Rad51 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on BLAST searches and sequence analysis documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Orthologs of the Dmc1 cofactors Mnd1 and Hop2 were identified in P. pacificus by homology searches.
source: Orthologs of the Dmc1 cofactors Mnd1 and Hop2 were also identified by homology searches (Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignments shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dmc1, Mnd1, and Hop2 are absent from both C. elegans and D. melanogaster.
source: By contrast, Dmc1/Mnd1/Hop2 are absent from both C. elegans and D. melanogaster, two model organisms that have evolved recombination-independent mechanisms of homolog pairing and synapsis (Villeneuve and Hillers, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Villeneuve and Hillers, 2001.

claim: Dmc1/Mnd1/Hop2 have been lost several times during the evolution of nematodes, including the entire Caenorhabditis genus and all sequenced members of Clade IV.
source: This analysis revealed that Dmc1/Mnd1/Hop2 have been lost several times during the evolution of nematodes, including the entire Caenorhabditis genus and all sequenced members of Clade IV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The recombinase Rad51 was detected in all nematode genomes examined.
source: As expected in light of its essential function in DNA repair, the recombinase Rad51 was detected in all genomes examined (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on genome sequence analysis, though the data are not shown.

claim: Homologs of HIM-8/ZIM family proteins were identified in many genome sequences from Clade V nematodes, but not in Pristionchus.
source: We identified homologs of these proteins in many of the genome sequences from Clade V nematodes, but not in Pristionchus.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence homology searches across nematode genomes.

claim: Disruption of either spo-11 or dmc-1 resulted in the detection of 12 DAPI-staining univalent chromosomes at diakinesis.
source: As expected, disruption of either spo-11 or dmc-1 resulted in the detection of 12 DAPI-staining univalent chromosomes at diakinesis, indicative of a failure in CO recombination (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytological data shown in Figure 5.

claim: rad-51 mutants were fertile and displayed only mild meiotic defects.
source: Surprisingly, rad-51 mutants were fertile and displayed only mild meiotic defects (see below).
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of rad-51 mutants, with detailed data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in spo-11 or dmc-1, but not rad-51, resulted in an obvious extension of the region of the germline displaying the crescent-shaped nuclear morphology characteristic of early meiosis.
source: Mutations in spo-11 or dmc-1, but not rad-51, resulted in an obvious extension of the region of the germline displaying the crescent-shaped nuclear morphology characteristic of early meiosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytological observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A similar 'extended transition zone' phenotype is seen in C. elegans mutants that fail to synapse their chromosomes during meiosis.
source: A similar 'extended transition zone' phenotype is seen in C. elegans mutants that fail to synapse their chromosomes during meiosis, suggesting that spo-11 and dmc-1 might be required for synapsis in P. pacificus.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about C. elegans meiotic mutants.

claim: In wild-type P. pacificus hermaphrodites, pairs of FISH signals for chromosomes X and IV remained far apart in zone 1, with average distances of 2.4 ± 1.0 μm and 2.5 ± 0.8 μm, respectively.
source: In zone 1 in wild-type P. pacificus hermaphrodites, which contains mostly proliferating germ cells, pairs of FISH signals remained far apart, with an average distance of 2.4 ± 1.0 μm (SD) and 2.5 ± 0.8 μm for chromosomes X and IV, respectively (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: In zone 2 of wild-type P. pacificus hermaphrodites, the average distances between homologous loci decreased significantly to 1.2 ± 1.1 μm and 1.1 ± 1.1 μm for chromosomes X and IV, respectively.
source: In zone 2, which spans the transition zone, the average distances between homologous loci decreased significantly (1.2 ± 1.1 μm and 1.1 ± 1.1 μm for probes on chromosomes X and IV, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Homologous FISH probes were more frequently separated in zones 4 and 5 in wild-type P. pacificus.
source: Surprisingly, homologous FISH probes were more frequently separated in zones 4 and 5 (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: In C. elegans, homologous loci remain closely apposed throughout an extended pachytene stage spanning most of the distal region of the gonad.
source: This differs from what is seen in C. elegans, where homologous loci remain closely apposed throughout an extended pachytene stage spanning most of the distal region (before the 'loop') of the gonad (MacQueen, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to MacQueen, 2002.

claim: Desynapsis initiates soon after completion of synapsis in P. pacificus, resulting in partial separation of homologs.
source: Together with our analysis of synapsis (below), this indicated that desynapsis initiates soon after completion of synapsis in P. pacificus, resulting in partial separation of homologs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from FISH data and synapsis analysis.

claim: The average distances between pairs of homologous FISH signals in spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants decreased markedly upon meiotic entry, although clearly less so than in wild type.
source: We noted that the average distances between pairs of homologous FISH signals in spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants also decreased markedly upon meiotic entry, although clearly less so than in wild type (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: rad-51 mutants showed distributions of probe distances more similar to wild-type animals.
source: In contrast, rad-51 mutants showed distributions of probe distances more similar to wild-type animals (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: FISH signals on different chromosomes were significantly closer to each other in the transition zone compared to premeiotic nuclei in both wild-type and mutant animals.
source: We observed that FISH signals on different chromosomes were also significantly closer to each other in the transition zone compared to premeiotic nuclei in both wild-type and mutant animals (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The distances between heterologous versus homologous pairs of FISH loci were not significantly different in spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants.
source: The distances between heterologous versus homologous pairs of FISH loci were not significantly different in spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants (p=0.1777 and p=0.6774, respectively, by Student's t-test), but homologous signals were clearly closer than heterologous signals in wild-type and rad-51 mutant animals (p<0.0001 by Student's t-test; Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of FISH data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Homologous signals were clearly closer than heterologous signals in wild-type and rad-51 mutant animals (p<0.0001).
source: The distances between heterologous versus homologous pairs of FISH loci were not significantly different in spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants (p=0.1777 and p=0.6774, respectively, by Student's t-test), but homologous signals were clearly closer than heterologous signals in wild-type and rad-51 mutant animals (p<0.0001 by Student's t-test; Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of FISH data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SPO-11 and DMC-1 are required for stable pairing and extended association of homologous loci throughout prophase in P. pacificus.
source: These data support the idea that clustering, rather than specific pairing, promotes proximity between both homologous and heterologous loci during leptotene/zygotene in spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants. Although we cannot conclude that transient homologous pairing is absent in these mutants, it is evident that these early recombination factors are required for stable pairing and extended association of homologous loci throughout prophase.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from FISH data comparing wild-type and mutant animals.

claim: rad-51 is dispensable for homolog pairing in P. pacificus, as in C. elegans.
source: In contrast, rad-51 is dispensable for homolog pairing, as in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is based on FISH data from rad-51 mutants and comparison to C. elegans.

claim: A gene encoding a HORMA domain protein most closely related to C. elegans HIM-3 was identified in the P. pacificus genome.
source: We identified a gene encoding a HORMA domain protein that is most closely related to C. elegans HIM-3 by reciprocal BLAST analysis (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis documented in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: A polyclonal antibody against Ppa-HOP-1 recognized chromosome axes from meiotic entry through late prophase.
source: Using genetic immunization, we raised a polyclonal antibody against a 100-amino acid segment of the predicted protein including part of the HORMA domain and found that it indeed recognized chromosome axes from meiotic entry through late prophase (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: SYP-4 was identified in P. pacificus based on a distinctive C-terminal domain containing several unusual motifs enriched in glycine and phenylalanine residues.
source: SYP-4 has a distinctive C-terminal domain containing several unusual motifs enriched in glycine and phenylalanine residues, which enabled us to identify it with confidence among the predicted proteins in P. pacificus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Immunofluorescence with an anti-HA antibody localized SYP-4::HA specifically between paired meiotic chromosomes, confirming SYP-4::HA as a marker for the SC.
source: We inserted an HA epitope tag at the C-terminus of the endogenous coding sequence and found that immunofluorescence with an epitope-specific antibody localized specifically between paired meiotic chromosomes, confirming SYP-4::HA as a useful marker for the SC (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: A likely P. pacificus ortholog of C. elegans SYP-1 has been identified, and an epitope-tagged allele displays an identical dynamic distribution to SYP-4.
source: A likely P. pacificus ortholog of C. elegans SYP-1 has also recently been identified, and an epitope-tagged allele displays an identical dynamic distribution (Kursel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kursel et al., 2021.

claim: The tagged SYP-4::HA protein supports normal meiosis, as indicated by the low percentage of inviable embryos and males among the progeny of homozygotes.
source: The tagged SYP-4::HA protein supports normal meiosis, as indicated by the low percentage of inviable embryos and males among the progeny of homozygotes (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by brood analysis data in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: HOP-1 was detected in the nucleoplasm in the premeiotic region of the germline and formed linear structures along chromosomes upon meiotic entry.
source: HOP-1 was detected in the nucleoplasm in the premeiotic region of the germline and formed linear structures along chromosomes upon meiotic entry.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: SYP-4 localized along chromosome segments shortly after meiotic entry, and fully colocalized with HOP-1 tracks during pachytene.
source: SYP-4 localized along chromosome segments shortly thereafter, and fully colocalized with HOP-1 tracks during pachytene.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The region of the germline containing nuclei with fully aligned stretches of SYP-4 and HOP-1 was very short in P. pacificus compared to C. elegans.
source: Notably, the region of the germline containing nuclei with fully aligned stretches of SYP-4 and HOP-1 was very short compared to C. elegans, in which SC disassembly occurs close to the bend of the gonad arm, shortly prior to diakinesis.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of immunofluorescence data between P. pacificus and C. elegans.

claim: SC disassembly initiated much earlier in P. pacificus than in C. elegans; the major fraction of prophase nuclei are thus in diplotene since chromosomes are only partially synapsed.
source: In contrast, SC disassembly initiated much earlier in P. pacificus; the major fraction of prophase nuclei are thus in diplotene since chromosomes are only partially synapsed.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Six short stretches of SYP-4 were apparent in diplotene nuclei in P. pacificus, which persisted over an extended region.
source: Six short stretches of SYP-4 were apparent in these nuclei, which persisted over an extended region (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The asymmetrical pattern of SC disassembly in P. pacificus is highly reminiscent of a more transient diplotene stage in C. elegans.
source: This asymmetrical pattern of SC disassembly is highly reminiscent of a more transient diplotene stage in C. elegans, in which the SC remains associated with one 'arm' of each homolog pair and subsequently contributes to the stepwise loss of cohesion during the meiotic divisions (Martinez-Perez et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to C. elegans data from Martinez-Perez et al., 2008.

claim: HOP-1 localized normally to chromosome axes in spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants, but extensive SC assembly failed.
source: HOP-1 localized normally to chromosome axes in spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants, but extensive SC assembly failed.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Small, dispersed puncta of SYP-4 were observed along chromosome axes in spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants, with occasional longer tracks.
source: Instead, small, dispersed puncta of SYP-4 were observed along chromosome axes, with occasional longer tracks (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The SYP-4 tracks in spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants represent nonhomologous synapsis.
source: They did not appear to associate preferentially with specific chromosomes, and our pairing analysis indicates that they represent nonhomologous synapsis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from immunofluorescence and FISH data.

claim: rad-51 mutants displayed robust synapsis with a distribution of stages similar to that seen in wild-type hermaphrodites.
source: In contrast to spo-11 and dmc-1 mutants, rad-51 mutants displayed robust synapsis with a distribution of stages similar to that seen in wild-type hermaphrodites (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Homologous synapsis depends on SPO-11 and DMC-1 in P. pacificus, in contrast to the recombination-independent synapsis seen in C. elegans.
source: These observations indicate that homologous synapsis depends on SPO-11 and DMC-1 in P. pacificus, in contrast to the recombination-independent synapsis seen in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from immunofluorescence data comparing wild-type and mutant animals, and comparison to C. elegans.

claim: DMC-1::V5 supported normal meiosis, as evidenced by a normal brood size, high embryonic viability, and low percentage of males.
source: DMC-1::V5 supported normal meiosis, as evidenced by a normal brood size, high embryonic viability, and low percentage of males (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by brood analysis data in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: DMC-1 and RAD-51 showed distinct and nonoverlapping patterns of localization in P. pacificus.
source: Surprisingly, the two proteins showed distinct and nonoverlapping patterns of localization.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4.

claim: DMC-1 localized very broadly along chromosomes in transition zone nuclei and disappeared immediately upon completion of synapsis.
source: DMC-1 localized very broadly along chromosomes in transition zone nuclei and disappeared immediately upon completion of synapsis.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: RAD-51 displayed a much more restricted, punctate distribution along chromosomes, which was only detected in nuclei in which DMC-1 no longer coated the chromosomes.
source: RAD-51 displayed a much more restricted, punctate distribution along chromosomes, which was only detected in nuclei in which DMC-1 no longer coated the chromosomes (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Occasional nuclei at the border between the transition zone and pachytene region exhibited both DMC-1 and RAD-51, although DMC-1 was very faint in these nuclei and did not overlap with RAD-51.
source: Occasional nuclei at the border between the transition zone and pachytene region exhibited both DMC-1 and RAD-51, although DMC-1 was very faint in these nuclei and did not overlap with RAD-51 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RAD-51::V5 supported normal meiosis, with a normal brood size, high embryonic viability, and low frequency of male self-progeny.
source: RAD-51::V5 also supported normal meiosis, with a normal brood size, high embryonic viability, and low frequency of male self-progeny (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by brood analysis data in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: DMC-1::V5 localization was normal in rad-51 mutants, indicating that RAD-51 does not play an essential role in the recruitment of DMC-1.
source: We did not detect RAD-51 in transition zone nuclei, where DMC-1 was abundant on chromatin, and we found that DMC-1::V5 localization was normal in rad-51 mutants, indicating that RAD-51 does not play an essential role in the recruitment of DMC-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In dmc-1 mutants, RAD-51 foci were detected only in late prophase nuclei, proximal to the very extended transition zone.
source: Conversely, in dmc-1 mutants we detected RAD-51 foci only in late prophase nuclei, proximal to the very extended transition zone (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RAD-51 foci were more abundant and larger in dmc-1 mutants than in wild-type pachytene nuclei.
source: RAD-51 foci were more abundant and larger in dmc-1 mutants than in wild-type pachytene nuclei, perhaps due to delays in repair due to the failure of homolog pairing and synapsis.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In spo-11 mutants, DMC-1 was restricted to one or a few nuclear aggregates rather than broadly along chromosomes.
source: Nevertheless, in spo-11 mutants DMC-1 was restricted to one or a few nuclear aggregates rather than broadly along chromosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: RAD-51 foci were absent from meiotic nuclei in spo-11 mutants.
source: Thus, it was unsurprising to see that RAD-51 foci were absent from meiotic nuclei in spo-11 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Some RAD-51 foci were observed in the mitotically proliferating region of the germline in spo-11 mutants, as in wild-type animals.
source: Some RAD-51 foci were observed in the mitotically proliferating region the germline in spo-11 mutants, as in wild-type animals, providing a positive control for immunofluorescence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: DMC-1 and RAD-51 bind to chromatin at distinct stages of meiotic prophase and are not interdependent, although both require DSBs for their localization to chromosomes.
source: Together these observations indicate that DMC-1 and RAD-51 bind to chromatin at distinct stages of meiotic prophase and are not interdependent, although both require DSBs for their localization to chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from immunofluorescence data in wild-type and mutant animals.

claim: Wild-type oocytes at diakinesis usually have six bivalents that can be resolved as discrete DAPI-staining bodies (average = 5.6).
source: Wild-type oocytes at this stage usually have six bivalents that can be resolved as discrete DAPI-staining bodies (average = 5.6), while in spo-11 mutants, ~12 DAPI-staining bodies were detected (average = 11.5), consistent with an absence of COs (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytological data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In spo-11 mutants, ~12 DAPI-staining bodies were detected at diakinesis (average = 11.5), consistent with an absence of COs.
source: Wild-type oocytes at this stage usually have six bivalents that can be resolved as discrete DAPI-staining bodies (average = 5.6), while in spo-11 mutants, ~12 DAPI-staining bodies were detected (average = 11.5), consistent with an absence of COs (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytological data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Oocytes at diakinesis were frequently absent in dmc-1 mutant germlines, indicative of a defect in meiotic progression and the likely activation of a checkpoint in response to unrepaired DSBs.
source: Interestingly, we frequently failed to detect oocytes at diakinesis in dmc-1 mutant germlines, indicative of a defect in meiotic progression and the likely activation of a checkpoint in response to unrepaired DSBs.
evidence: The claim is based on cytological observations and inference about checkpoint activation.

claim: In dmc-1 mutants, when diakinesis nuclei were observed, an average of 11.6 DAPI-staining bodies were detected, reflecting an absence of COs.
source: In cases when we did see nuclei at diakinesis, we observed an average of 11.6 DAPI-staining bodies, reflecting an absence of COs, as in spo-11 mutants (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytological data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Disruption of rad-51 resulted in homozygous mutant hermaphrodites that were viable and fertile, although animals produced smaller broods and their embryos showed greatly reduced viability.
source: Unexpectedly, disruption of rad-51 resulted in homozygous mutant hermaphrodites that were viable and fertile, although animals produced smaller broods and their embryos showed greatly reduced viability, likely due to an inability to repair damage arising during DNA replication (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by brood analysis data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: RAD-51 is essential for completion of meiosis in most organisms where it has been examined.
source: This was surprising because RAD-51 is essential for completion of meiosis in most organisms where it has been examined.
evidence: This is established knowledge from studies in other organisms.

claim: Homozygous rad-51 mutant gonads displayed diakinesis nuclei more frequently than dmc-1 mutants, although they were absent in 2 out of 20 gonads scored.
source: Homozygous rad-51 mutant gonads also displayed diakinesis nuclei more frequently than dmc-1 mutants, although they were absent in 2 out of 20 gonads scored, indicating that loss of DMC-1 function impairs meiotic progression more severely than loss of RAD-51 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytological data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Loss of DMC-1 function impairs meiotic progression more severely than loss of RAD-51.
source: Homozygous rad-51 mutant gonads also displayed diakinesis nuclei more frequently than dmc-1 mutants, although they were absent in 2 out of 20 gonads scored, indicating that loss of DMC-1 function impairs meiotic progression more severely than loss of RAD-51 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cytological observations comparing dmc-1 and rad-51 mutants.

claim: Self-fertilizing rad-51 mutants had a lower average brood size than wild-type hermaphrodites, and dmc-1 mutants had even smaller broods, ranging from 0 to 35 embryos laid per mutant homozygote.
source: Consistent with this observation, while self-fertilizing rad-51 mutants had a lower average brood size than wild-type hermaphrodites, dmc-1 mutants had even smaller broods, ranging from 0 to 35 embryos laid per mutant homozygote (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by brood analysis data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: C. elegans rad-51 mutants display chromatin aggregates and fragments at diakinesis.
source: In striking contrast to C. elegans rad-51 mutants, which display chromatin aggregates and fragments at diakinesis (Martin et al., 2005; Rinaldo et al., 2002), Ppa-rad-51 mutants displayed an average of six DAPI-staining bodies, similar to wild-type (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martin et al., 2005 and Rinaldo et al., 2002.

claim: Ppa-rad-51 mutants displayed an average of six DAPI-staining bodies at diakinesis, similar to wild-type.
source: In striking contrast to C. elegans rad-51 mutants, which display chromatin aggregates and fragments at diakinesis (Martin et al., 2005; Rinaldo et al., 2002), Ppa-rad-51 mutants displayed an average of six DAPI-staining bodies, similar to wild-type (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytological data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RAD-51 does not play an essential role in CO formation in P. pacificus.
source: Together with the relatively high viability of progeny of rad-51 homozygous mutants, this indicates that RAD-51 does not play an essential role in CO formation in P. pacificus.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cytological and brood analysis data.

claim: The strain expressing COSA-1::3xFLAG yielded progeny with high embryonic viability and few males, indicating that the tagged protein supports normal meiosis.
source: The strain expressing COSA-1::3xFLAG yielded progeny with high embryonic viability and few males, indicating that the tagged protein supports normal meiosis (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by brood analysis data in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: COSA-1 foci were detected along the SC beginning as early as zygotene, which decreased in number and became brighter within the short pachytene region.
source: Immunostaining with anti-FLAG antibodies revealed discrete foci along the SC, beginning as early as zygotene, which decreased in number and became brighter within the short pachytene region (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Most pachytene nuclei displayed six COSA-1 foci, each of which was associated with an individual SC, indicating the presence of a single designated CO site between each pair of homologs.
source: Most pachytene nuclei displayed six COSA-1 foci, each of which was associated with an individual SC, indicating the presence of a single designated CO site between each pair of homologs (Figure 6C and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—video 1.

claim: Pachytene spermatocytes in J4 larval-stage hermaphrodites also displayed approximately six COSA-1 foci.
source: We stained J4 larval-stage hermaphrodites whose germlines had not yet undergone the switch from spermatogenesis to oogenesis and found that pachytene spermatocytes also displayed approximately six COSA-1 foci (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: P. pacificus, like C. elegans, has robust chromosome-wide CO interference in both spermatogenesis and oogenesis.
source: This suggests that P. pacificus, like C. elegans, has robust chromosome-wide CO interference in both spermatogenesis and oogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from COSA-1 foci counts in spermatocytes and oocytes.

claim: SC disassembly in P. pacificus appeared to be regulated by the position of the designated CO site, as in C. elegans.
source: Intriguingly, SC disassembly appeared to be regulated by the position of the designated CO site, as in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations and comparison to C. elegans.

claim: By mid-prophase, six short stretches of SYP-4::HA were observed, each associated with a single COSA-1::3xFLAG focus near one end.
source: By mid-prophase, six short stretches of SYP-4::HA were observed, each associated with a single COSA-1::3xFLAG focus near one end (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: As meiosis progressed further, COSA-1::3xFLAG foci became undetectable, although short stretches of SYP-4::HA could still be observed.
source: As meiosis progressed further, COSA-1::3xFLAG foci became undetectable, although short stretches of SYP-4::HA could still be observed.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Splaying of chromosome axes was observed along the 'long arms' on one side of the COSA-1 focus upon disappearance of the SC from those regions.
source: We also observed splaying of chromosome axes along the 'long arms' on one side of the COSA-1 focus upon disappearance of the SC from those regions (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HOP-1 was retained on both arms following SC disassembly, although the signal appeared fainter along the long arms.
source: HOP-1 was retained on both arms following SC disassembly, although the signal appeared fainter along the long arms, perhaps due to separation of the two axes.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Short stretches of SYP-4::HA colocalize with corresponding bright stretches of HOP-1 during late diplotene.
source: At this stage, short stretches of SYP-4::HA colocalize with corresponding bright stretches of HOP-1 (Figures 3B and 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3B and 6D.

claim: Bivalents at diakinesis and meiotic metaphase I displayed a cruciform structure similar to that seen in C. elegans, consistent with a single chiasma per chromosome pair.
source: Bivalents at diakinesis and meiotic metaphase I also displayed a cruciform structure similar to that seen in C. elegans, consistent with a single chiasma per chromosome pair (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytological observations shown in Figure 1C and comparison to C. elegans.

claim: In C. elegans, the orientation of chromosomes during meiotic segregation is stochastically determined by the position of the single CO between each pair.
source: In C. elegans, the orientation of chromosomes during meiotic segregation is stochastically determined by the position of the single CO between each pair: the 'long arm,' where SC first disassembles, is designated to retain cohesion and to lead towards the poles while the 'short arm' releases cohesion during MI, but then becomes the leading end for segregation of chromatids during meiosis II (Albertson and Thomson, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Albertson and Thomson, 1993.

claim: In P. pacificus, an asymmetrically localized FISH probe localized to either the long (desynapsed) arm or the short arm in different nuclei, similar to C. elegans.
source: Using FISH to mark specific chromosome regions together with immunostaining of SYP-4::HA, we found that the same was true for P. pacificus: an asymmetrically localized probe localized to either the long (desynapsed) arm or the short arm in different nuclei (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: dmc-1 mutants showed a complete absence of COSA-1 foci throughout prophase.
source: As expected, dmc-1 mutants showed a complete absence of COSA-1 foci throughout prophase, while six foci were observed in pachytene nuclei in rad-51 mutants (Figure 7A), consistent with the number of DAPI-staining bodies observed at diakinesis in these mutants (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Six COSA-1 foci were observed in pachytene nuclei in rad-51 mutants, consistent with the number of DAPI-staining bodies observed at diakinesis.
source: As expected, dmc-1 mutants showed a complete absence of COSA-1 foci throughout prophase, while six foci were observed in pachytene nuclei in rad-51 mutants (Figure 7A), consistent with the number of DAPI-staining bodies observed at diakinesis in these mutants (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A and cytological data in Figure 5B.

claim: A few bright COSA-1::3xFLAG foci were present throughout prophase in spo-11 mutants.
source: A few bright COSA-1::3xFLAG foci were present throughout prophase in spo-11 mutants (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The COSA-1 foci in spo-11 mutants do not mark designated COs.
source: However, since ~12 DAPI-staining bodies were observed during diakinesis, we conclude that these COSA-1 foci do not mark designated COs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from immunofluorescence and cytological data.

claim: A similar phenomenon of COSA-1 foci in the absence of bona fide recombination intermediates has been reported in C. elegans spo-11 mutants.
source: A similar phenomenon has been reported in C. elegans spo-11 mutants (Nadarajan et al., 2017; Pattabiraman et al., 2017), suggesting that COSA-1 and other CO factors can coalesce at sites lacking bona fide recombination intermediates when such structures are absent.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nadarajan et al., 2017 and Pattabiraman et al., 2017.

claim: The Sommer lab initially concluded that the map length of each P. pacificus chromosome exceeded 100 cM, with a maximum length of 215 cM for chromosome I.
source: By summing over measured genetic intervals on the same linkage group, the Sommer lab initially concluded that the map length of each chromosome exceeded 100 cM, with a maximum length of 215 cM for chromosome I, which is also physically the longest (Hong and Sommer, 2006; Srinivasan et al., 2003; Srinivasan et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hong and Sommer, 2006; Srinivasan et al., 2003; and Srinivasan et al., 2002.

claim: A map derived by the Sommer lab based on RNA sequencing of ~F10 recombinant inbred lines yielded markedly shorter genetic lengths, below 100 cM per chromosome.
source: However, a map derived by the same group based on RNA sequencing of~ F10 recombinant inbred lines (RILs) yielded markedly shorter genetic lengths, below 100 cM per chromosome (Rödelsperger et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rödelsperger et al., 2017.

claim: A total of 93 progeny from a cross between CA/WA hybrid males and CA/LR hybrid hermaphrodites were sequenced for genetic map construction.
source: A total of 93 progeny from a cross between CA/WA hybrid males and CA/LR hybrid hermaphrodites were sequenced (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: The crossing strategy allowed simultaneous mapping of COs that occur during hermaphrodite oogenesis and male spermatogenesis from the same progeny.
source: This strategy allowed us to simultaneously map COs that occur during hermaphrodite oogenesis and male spermatogenesis from the same progeny (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: The map lengths for each chromosome are close to 50 cM for both oocyte and spermatocyte meiosis, very similar to genetic map lengths in C. elegans.
source: First, the map lengths for each chromosome are close to 50 cM for both oocyte and spermatocyte meiosis, very similar to genetic map lengths in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic map data shown in Figure 8C and comparison to C. elegans.

claim: A single CO usually occurs between each pair of chromosomes per meiosis in P. pacificus, consistent with cytological observations.
source: This indicates that a single CO usually occurs between each pair of chromosomes per meiosis, consistent with our cytological observations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic map data and cytological observations.

claim: Close to half of all chromatids inherited from each parent were nonrecombinant as expected if a single CO occurs between two of the four possible chromatids.
source: Close to half of all chromatids inherited from each parent were nonrecombinant as expected if a single CO occurs between two of the four possible chromatids.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of genetic map data.

claim: A few examples of double COs were observed in the genetic map data, but such events were rare (6/1012 chromatids), and were most prevalent on the longest chromosome (chromosome I).
source: We did observe a few examples of double COs in our data, but such events were rare (6/1012 chromatids), and were most prevalent on the longest chromosome (chromosome I; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of genetic map data documented in Supplementary file 5.

claim: The distal regions ('arms') of P. pacificus chromosomes show higher recombination rates than the central regions, as in Caenorhabditis.
source: Second, the distal regions ('arms') show higher recombination rates than the central regions of each chromosome, as in Caenorhabditis (Barnes et al., 1995; Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on genetic map data shown in Figure 8C and citations to Barnes et al., 1995 and Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009.

claim: The bias for COs on chromosome arms was also evident in a map constructed using RNA sequencing data.
source: This bias was also evident in a map constructed using RNA sequencing data (Rödelsperger et al., 2017) and seems to be a widely conserved feature among Rhabditids and perhaps other nematode clades (Doyle et al., 2018; Gonzalez de la Rosa et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rödelsperger et al., 2017; Doyle et al., 2018; and Gonzalez de la Rosa et al., 2021.

claim: The male spermatocyte map showed a pronounced asymmetry for chromosomes III and IV, with COs occurring predominantly on one arm, whereas the corresponding oocyte maps show COs on both arms.
source: Third, the male spermatocyte map showed a pronounced asymmetry for chromosomes III and IV, with COs occurring predominantly on one arm, whereas the corresponding oocyte maps show COs on both arms.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic map data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The oocyte-specific map for the X chromosome shows an absence of COs on the right arm.
source: Conversely, the oocyte-specific map for the X chromosome shows an absence of COs on the right arm (the single X chromosome does not undergo COs during male spermatogenesis; Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is based on genetic map data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: COs were suppressed on one side of chromosomes III, IV, and X in the hybrid parents, likely reflecting structural rearrangements between the parental strains.
source: These findings suggest that COs were suppressed on one side of these chromosomes in the hybrid parents. This suppression may reflect structural rearrangements between the parental strains.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic map data.

claim: There are predicted structural differences between the Washington and California versions of chromosomes III and IV, and between the La Réunion and California versions of the X chromosome.
source: Specifically, we predict that there are structural differences between the Washington and California versions of chromosomes III and IV, and between the La Réunion and California versions of the X chromosome.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic map data showing CO suppression.

claim: A lack of COs on the right arm of the X chromosome was also evident in data from RILs from a cross between the same strains from La Réunion and California.
source: A lack of COs on the right arm of the X chromosome was also evident in data from RILs from a cross between the same strains from La Réunion and California (Rödelsperger et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rödelsperger et al., 2017.

claim: The CO suppression on chromosomes III and IV in WA/CA hybrid spermatocytes likely reflects intra- rather than inter-chromosomal rearrangements.
source: The CO suppression on chromosomes III and IV in WA/CA hybrid spermatocytes likely reflects intra- rather than inter-chromosomal rearrangements since the data do not show pseudolinkage of loci on these chromosomes, as would be expected if a III; IV translocation were present.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic map data.

claim: The asymmetry in CO suppression suggests that one arm of each chromosome may contain a region that plays a dominant role in CO formation during meiosis.
source: Notably, the asymmetry in CO suppression also suggests that one arm of each chromosome may contain a region that plays a dominant role in CO formation during meiosis, perhaps related to the function of PCs in C. elegans (see Discussion for more details).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic map data and speculation about PC function.

claim: Pronounced segregation distortion was detected for chromosomes I and II in the oocyte map, with inheritance of the La Réunion haplotype strongly favored.
source: Finally, we detected pronounced segregation distortion for chromosomes I and II in the oocyte map, with inheritance of the La Réunion haplotype strongly favored (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on genetic map data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nonrecombinant chromosomes of the La Réunion haplotype were inherited about eightfold more frequently than the nonrecombinant California chromatids for chromosomes I and II.
source: In each case nonrecombinant chromosomes of the La Réunion haplotype were inherited about eightfold more frequently than the nonrecombinant California chromatids.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic map data.

claim: The segregation distortion observations are consistent with either a bias in meiosis segregation (meiotic drive) or the presence of loci on these chromosomes that cause genetic incompatibilities.
source: These observations are consistent with either a bias in meiosis segregation – that is, meiotic drive – or the presence of loci on these chromosomes that cause genetic incompatibilities (i.e., inviability of some F2 progeny).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic map data.

claim: Analysis of recombinant chromatids suggests that genetic incompatibilities are more likely than meiotic drive to explain the segregation distortion.
source: Analysis of recombinant chromatids suggests that the latter scenario is more likely since a gradient in the severity of the distortion can be detected along the physical length of the chromosomes, consistent with the idea that specific loci on the affected autosomes may be toxic to hybrid progeny; it is more difficult to imagine how specific loci could lead to meiotic drive in a holocentric species.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic map data and reasoning about holocentric chromosomes.

claim: Dmc1 is uniquely required during meiosis.
source: However, Dmc1 is uniquely required during meiosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge from studies in other organisms.

claim: The distinct requirements for Rad51 and Dmc1 are thought to be due in part to the activity of Dmc1-specific cofactors Mnd1 and Hop2, which confer different activities, and/or a higher tolerance for mismatches by Dmc1.
source: The distinct requirements for Rad51 and Dmc1 are thought to be due in part to the activity of Dmc1-specific cofactors Mnd1 and Hop2, which confer different activities, and/or a higher tolerance for mismatches by Dmc1, which may enable it to promote recombination between nonidentical homologs (Steinfeld et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Steinfeld et al., 2019.

claim: The abundance of DMC-1 foci suggests that it binds to sites other than repair intermediates.
source: The binding of these proteins to chromatin appears very different; the abundance of DMC-1 foci suggests that it binds to sites other than repair intermediates.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from immunofluorescence data.

claim: RAD-51 displays a more restricted punctate localization, and only after DMC-1 is largely removed from chromosomes upon completion of synapsis.
source: In contrast, RAD-51 displays a more restricted punctate localization, and only after DMC-1 is largely removed from chromosomes upon completion of synapsis.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both DMC-1 and RAD-51 depend on SPO-11 for their association with meiotic chromosomes.
source: Intriguingly, both DMC-1 and RAD-51 depend on SPO-11 for their association with meiotic chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data in spo-11 mutants shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: DMC-1 is positively regulated by a mechanism that responds to SPO-11 activity, likely through activation of a DNA damage signaling pathway.
source: We interpret these observations to indicate that DMC-1 is positively regulated by a mechanism that responds to SPO-11 activity, likely through activation of a DNA damage signaling pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from immunofluorescence data in spo-11 mutants.

claim: The association of RAD-51 with recombination intermediates may normally be inhibited until after the establishment of CO intermediates between each pair of chromosomes.
source: In contrast, the association of RAD-51 with recombination intermediates may normally be inhibited until after the establishment of CO intermediates between each pair of chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the sequential localization of DMC-1 and RAD-51.

claim: In budding yeast and A. thaliana, RAD-51 acts as an accessory protein for DMC-1 nucleofilament formation.
source: In S. cerevisiae and A. thaliana, Dmc1 functions as an essential catalyst for interhomolog JM formation during meiotic DSB repair, while Rad51 acts as an accessory protein for Dmc1 nucleofilament formation (Cloud et al., 2012; Da Ines et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cloud et al., 2012 and Da Ines et al., 2013.

claim: RAD-51 in P. pacificus is dispensable for the activity of DMC-1 in pairing, synapsis, and CO formation.
source: In contrast to budding yeast and A. thaliana, we have found that RAD-51 in P. pacificus is dispensable for the activity of DMC-1 in pairing, synapsis, and CO formation.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of rad-51 mutants showing normal pairing, synapsis, and CO formation.

claim: RAD-51 appears to play a supporting role in DSB repair during pachytene, promoting repair of DSBs that remain after CO designation has occurred.
source: Instead, RAD-51 appears to play a supporting role in DSB repair during pachytene, promoting repair of DSBs that remain after CO designation has occurred.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the timing of RAD-51 localization and the phenotype of rad-51 mutants.

claim: In C. elegans, a switch between two modes of DSB repair is observed during meiotic prophase, with association of RAD-51 with repair intermediates differentially regulated from the onset of meiosis until a mid-pachytene transition that coincides with CO designation.
source: In C. elegans, which expresses only RAD-51, a similar switch between two modes of DSB repair is nevertheless observed during meiotic prophase: association of RAD-51 with repair intermediates is differentially regulated from the onset of meiosis until a mid-pachytene transition that coincides with CO designation; at this time, competence to convert DSBs to interhomolog COs is also lost (Hayashi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hayashi et al., 2007.

claim: An analogous switch from a 'meiotic' repair to a 'somatic'-like repair pathway in mid-pachytene has been described in mouse spermatocytes.
source: An analogous switch from a 'meiotic' repair to a 'somatic'-like repair pathway in mid-pachytene has also been described in mouse spermatocytes (Enguita-Marruedo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Enguita-Marruedo et al., 2019.

claim: DMC-1 and RAD-51 have specialized functions in P. pacificus: formation of interhomolog CO intermediates by DMC-1 prior to completion of synapsis, followed by a more generic mode of DSB repair mediated by RAD-51.
source: Taken together, it appears that DMC-1 and RAD-51 have specialized functions in P. pacificus: formation of interhomolog CO intermediates by DMC-1 prior to completion of synapsis, followed by a more generic mode of DSB repair mediated by RAD-51.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the analysis of DMC-1 and RAD-51 localization and mutant phenotypes.

claim: Nuclei in rad-51 mutants display cruciform bivalents and lack fragmented chromatin at diakinesis, suggesting that excess DSBs can be repaired through an alternate pathway that does not depend on RAD-51 activity, or that DMC-1 can compensate for loss of RAD-51.
source: Our observations that nuclei in rad-51 mutants display cruciform bivalents and lack fragmented chromatin at diakinesis suggest that excess DSBs can be repaired through an alternate pathway that does not depend on RAD-51 activity, such as non-homologous end joining, or that DMC-1 can compensate for loss of RAD-51 but not vice versa.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cytological observations in rad-51 mutants and speculation about repair pathways.

claim: Recombination-independent homologous synapsis in C. elegans relies on PCs, specialized chromosome regions that interact with nuclear envelope and drive chromosome movement during early prophase.
source: A body of prior work has revealed that recombination-independent homologous synapsis in C. elegans relies on PCs, specialized chromosome regions that interact with nuclear envelope and drive chromosome movement during early prophase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans meiosis.

claim: PCs in C. elegans mediate synapsis-independent pairing and also act as the sites of synapsis initiation.
source: PCs in C. elegans mediate synapsis-independent pairing and also act as the sites of synapsis initiation (MacQueen et al., 2005; Rog and Dernburg, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to MacQueen et al., 2005 and Rog and Dernburg, 2013.

claim: In most other organisms, telomere-led chromosome movement is thought to promote homologous interactions, but stabilization of pairing and initiation of synapsis require and often occur at early recombination intermediates, which depend on Spo11 and Dmc1.
source: In most other organisms, telomere-led chromosome movement is thought to promote homologous interactions, but stabilization of pairing and initiation of synapsis require and often occur at early recombination intermediates, which depend on Spo11 and Dmc1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about meiosis in other organisms.

claim: PC activity in C. elegans depends on and is largely defined by the recruitment of a family of zinc finger proteins that bind to DNA sequence motifs in these regions.
source: PC activity in C. elegans depends on and is largely defined by the recruitment of a family of zinc finger proteins that bind to DNA sequence motifs in these regions (Phillips et al., 2009b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Phillips et al., 2009b.

claim: The zinc finger proteins ZIM-1, ZIM-2, ZIM-3, and HIM-8 in C. elegans act as scaffolds to recruit a cascade of kinase activities required for pairing and synapsis.
source: These proteins, known as ZIM-1, ZIM-2, ZIM-3, and HIM-8 in C. elegans, act as scaffolds to recruit a cascade of kinase activities required for pairing and synapsis (Harper et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2015; Labella et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harper et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2015; and Labella et al., 2011.

claim: Many of the sequenced genomes of nematodes in Clade V include homologs of the HIM-8/ZIM family as well as Dmc1, Hop2, and Mnd1.
source: We found it intriguing that many of the sequenced genomes of nematodes in Clade V include homologs of the HIM-8/ZIM family as well as Dmc1, Hop2, and Mnd1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Pristionchus genus is unusual within Clade V in that it lacks apparent homologs of the PC proteins.
source: The Pristionchus genus is unusual within this Clade in that it lacks apparent homologs of the PC proteins, while Caenorhabditis is among the few genera that lack Dmc1/Mnd1/Hop2, although these genes were independently lost along the branch leading to Oscheius tipulae.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Caenorhabditis is among the few genera that lack Dmc1/Mnd1/Hop2, although these genes were independently lost along the branch leading to Oscheius tipulae.
source: The Pristionchus genus is unusual within this Clade in that it lacks apparent homologs of the PC proteins, while Caenorhabditis is among the few genera that lack Dmc1/Mnd1/Hop2, although these genes were independently lost along the branch leading to Oscheius tipulae.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is unlikely that PC proteins arose as an alternative to DMC-1 function in meiosis, although in Caenorhabditis they may have acquired a synapsis initiation activity that eventually allowed degeneration and loss of DMC-1.
source: Because these homologs are present in species that retain intact DMC-1 genes, it is unlikely that PC proteins arose as an alternative to DMC-1 function in meiosis, although in Caenorhabditis they may have acquired a synapsis initiation activity that eventually allowed degeneration and loss of DMC-1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from phylogenetic analysis and speculation about evolutionary history.

claim: The phylogenetic analysis suggests that the ability of PCs to promote homologous synapsis in the absence of DSBs and strand invasion may be recently derived, and perhaps restricted to Caenorhabditis.
source: Our phylogenetic analysis suggests that the ability of PCs to promote homologous synapsis in the absence of DSBs and strand invasion may be recently derived, and perhaps restricted to Caenorhabditis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The existence of PCs in C. elegans was initially inferred because chromosome rearrangements often result in asymmetric CO suppression.
source: The existence of PCs in C. elegans was initially inferred because chromosome rearrangements often result in asymmetric CO suppression: regions distal to translocation breakpoints are inhibited from crossing over, while the chromosome region containing the PC undergoes elevated recombination due to a feedback mechanism that helps to ensure an 'obligate crossover' (Rose and McKIM, 1992; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rose and McKIM, 1992 and Yu et al., 2016.

claim: The asymmetric CO suppression detected in the genetic map data suggests that a directional CO-promoting activity may be located near one end of each chromosome in P. pacificus.
source: The asymmetric CO suppression we detected in our genetic map data suggests that a directional CO-promoting activity may also be located near one end of each chromosome in P. pacificus.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic map data and comparison to C. elegans.

claim: If PCs are conserved in P. pacificus, they clearly do not mediate recombination-independent synapsis, as in C. elegans.
source: If PCs are indeed conserved in P. pacificus, they clearly do not mediate recombination-independent synapsis, as in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cytological observations showing dependence of synapsis on SPO-11 and DMC-1.

claim: Based on cytological observations, it is more likely that synapsis initiates at recombination intermediates in P. pacificus.
source: Based on our cytological observations, it is more likely that synapsis initiates at recombination intermediates in P. pacificus, although this has not yet been tested rigorously.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cytological data, though not yet rigorously tested.

claim: Unique PC regions may have arisen in holocentric nematodes as part of a meiotic system that promotes karyotype stability.
source: We have previously speculated that unique PC regions may have arisen in holocentric nematodes as part of a meiotic system that promotes karyotype stability (MacQueen et al., 2005; Rog and Dernburg, 2013), an idea that seems more viable in light of our indirect evidence for their conservation in Pristionchus.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to MacQueen et al., 2005 and Rog and Dernburg, 2013, and indirect evidence from this study.

claim: The existence of a PC-based mechanism could potentially account for the preservation of genetic linkage units known as 'Nigon elements' over long evolutionary periods.
source: The existence of such a mechanism could potentially account for the preservation of genetic linkage units known as 'Nigon elements' over long evolutionary periods, which has been documented through genome sequencing of diverse nematodes (Foster et al., 2020; Gonzalez de la Rosa et al., 2021; Tandonnet et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and citations to Foster et al., 2020; Gonzalez de la Rosa et al., 2021; and Tandonnet et al., 2019.

claim: P. pacificus shares many experimental advantages with C. elegans for molecular studies of meiosis.
source: P. pacificus shares many experimental advantages with C. elegans for molecular studies of meiosis.
evidence: This is based on the authors' assessment of the experimental system.

claim: Genome engineering using CRISPR/Cas9 is less efficient in P. pacificus than in C. elegans.
source: Genome engineering using CRISPR/Cas9 is less efficient than in C. elegans, and has so far been refractory to large insertions, such as transgenes encoding fluorescent proteins.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experience with genome editing in P. pacificus.

claim: The recombination landscape is remarkably well conserved between P. pacificus and C. elegans.
source: Our work has now established that the recombination landscape is remarkably well conserved between P. pacificus and C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of genetic map data between P. pacificus and C. elegans.

claim: Enrichment of COs on the chromosome arms and robust chromosome-wide CO interference can be implemented through divergent meiotic programs.
source: Indeed, comparison of P. pacificus and C. elegans reveals that enrichment of COs on the chromosome arms and robust chromosome-wide CO interference can be implemented through divergent meiotic programs, for example, with synapsis either dependent on or independent of CO precursors, and with CO sites designated either before or after completion of synapsis.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of meiotic mechanisms between P. pacificus and C. elegans.

claim: Other features of chromosome organization, including enrichment for novel and developmentally regulated genes on the arms, with more ancestral and broadly expressed genes concentrated in the centers, as well as chromosome-wide chromatin modification profiles, are also conserved across the Rhabditina.
source: Interestingly, other features of chromosome organization, including enrichment for novel and developmentally regulated genes on the arms, with more ancestral and broadly expressed genes concentrated in the centers, as well as chromosome-wide chromatin modification profiles, are also conserved across the Rhabditina (Werner et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Werner et al., 2018.

claim: The conservation of genomic features over tens of millions of years of evolution suggests that they are important for genome transmission and/or function.
source: How the recombination landscape is shaped by and/or contributes to these genomic features is not well understood, but the conservation of these features over tens of millions of years of evolution suggests that they are important for genome transmission and/or function.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the conservation of genomic features.

claim: Most and perhaps all nematode species have holocentric chromosomes.
source: Nematodes are an ancient and widespread phylum in which most and perhaps all species have holocentric chromosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nematodes.

claim: The presence of spindle-attachment sites along the length of chromosomes poses unique challenges for both mitosis and meiosis.
source: The presence of spindle-attachment sites along the length of chromosomes poses unique challenges for both mitosis and meiosis (Dernburg, 2001; Melters et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dernburg, 2001 and Melters et al., 2012.

claim: In monocentric organisms, the centromeres and/or pericentromeric regions typically recruit factors such as Shugoshin to maintain cohesion between sister chromatids during the first, reductional meiotic division.
source: In monocentric organisms, the centromeres and/or pericentromeric regions typically recruit factors such as Shugoshin to maintain cohesion between sister chromatids during the first, reductional meiotic division, while release of cohesion along chromosome arms allows segregation of recombinant homologs (Watanabe and Kitajima, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Watanabe and Kitajima, 2005.

claim: Holocentric chromosomes must use alternate mechanisms to implement the stepwise loss of cohesion needed for two orderly meiotic divisions.
source: Holocentric chromosomes must use alternate mechanisms to implement the stepwise loss of cohesion needed for two orderly meiotic divisions.
evidence: This is based on inference from the structure of holocentric chromosomes.

claim: The asymmetric SC disassembly observed in P. pacificus likely reflects conservation of a mechanism discovered in C. elegans in which CO designation leads to asymmetric SC disassembly, retention of cohesion on one side of the CO site during the first division, and release on the other side.
source: The asymmetric SC disassembly we observe in P. pacificus, together with our evidence that the orientation of chromosomes during meiotic divisions is stochastically determined by CO position (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) likely reflects conservation of a mechanism discovered in C. elegans in which CO designation leads to asymmetric SC disassembly, retention of cohesion on one side of the CO site during the first division, and release on the other side (Ferrandiz et al., 2018; Martinez-Perez et al., 2008; Severson and Meyer, 2014; Tzur et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cytological observations and citations to Ferrandiz et al., 2018; Martinez-Perez et al., 2008; Severson and Meyer, 2014; and Tzur et al., 2012.

claim: This particular solution to the problem of segregating holocentric chromosomes in meiosis appears to predate the Rhabditine radiation.
source: Thus, this particular solution to the problem of segregating holocentric chromosomes in meiosis appears to predate the Rhabditine radiation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the conservation of asymmetric SC disassembly between P. pacificus and C. elegans.

claim: This pathway relies on the formation of two bivalent 'arms' with reciprocal functions, which in turn depends on strict CO interference; multiple COs 'confuse' the system and lead to frequent missegregation.
source: This pathway relies on the formation of two bivalent 'arms' with reciprocal functions, which in turn depends on strict CO interference; multiple COs 'confuse' the system and lead to frequent missegregation (Hollis et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hollis et al., 2020.

claim: These two features of meiosis (asymmetric SC disassembly and strict CO interference) are expected to be widely shared among and perhaps beyond Clade V nematodes.
source: We expect that these two features of meiosis are widely shared among and perhaps beyond Clade V nematodes.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the conservation observed between P. pacificus and C. elegans.

claim: Studies in Ascarids have shown that heterochromatic regions near one end of a chromosome act as meiotic centromeres and are eliminated in somatic cells.
source: However, they may not be universal among nematodes; for example, studies in Ascarids have shown that heterochromatic regions near one end of a chromosome act as meiotic centromeres and are eliminated in somatic cells (Goday and Pimpinelli, 1989; Melters et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goday and Pimpinelli, 1989 and Melters et al., 2012.

claim: The mechanism in Ascarids may allow for more relaxed CO control and/or a different pattern of COs between homologous chromosomes.
source: This mechanism may allow for more relaxed CO control and/or a different pattern of COs between homologous chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the implications of the Ascarid mechanism.

claim: P. pacificus is an androdioecious species, with populations consisting of self-fertilizing hermaphrodites (XX) and a low frequency of spontaneous males (XO).
source: Like its distant relative C. elegans, P. pacificus is an androdioecious species, with populations consisting of self-fertilizing hermaphrodites (XX) and a low frequency of spontaneous males (XO) (Sommer, 2015; Sommer et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sommer, 2015 and Sommer et al., 1996.

claim: P. pacificus has a short life cycle of 3.5 days at 20°C.
source: P. pacificus also shares with C. elegans a short life cycle of 3.5 days at 20°C, produces large broods of about 200 progeny by self-fertilization, and is easily cultured in the lab (Hong and Sommer, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hong and Sommer, 2006.

claim: P. pacificus produces large broods of about 200 progeny by self-fertilization.
source: P. pacificus also shares with C. elegans a short life cycle of 3.5 days at 20°C, produces large broods of about 200 progeny by self-fertilization, and is easily cultured in the lab (Hong and Sommer, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hong and Sommer, 2006.

claim: P. pacificus is easily cultured in the lab.
source: P. pacificus also shares with C. elegans a short life cycle of 3.5 days at 20°C, produces large broods of about 200 progeny by self-fertilization, and is easily cultured in the lab (Hong and Sommer, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hong and Sommer, 2006.

claim: The morphology and organization of the P. pacificus germline are very similar to that of C. elegans.
source: The morphology and organization of the P. pacificus germline are very similar to that of C. elegans.
evidence: This is based on the authors' cytological observations.

claim: Hermaphrodites of P. pacificus have two tubelike gonad arms in which sperm and ova are produced sequentially, while males have a single arm.
source: Hermaphrodites have two tubelike gonad arms in which sperm and ova are produced sequentially, while males have a single arm (Rudel et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rudel et al., 2005.

claim: The gonads of P. pacificus are organized as a cylindrical monolayer of cells abutting a central core, or rachis.
source: These are organized as a cylindrical monolayer of cells abutting a central core, or rachis.
evidence: This is based on the authors' cytological observations.

claim: The distal tip of the P. pacificus gonad is populated by proliferating germline stem cells.
source: The distal tip is populated by proliferating germline stem cells (Figure 1A, B and D), as confirmed by the incorporation of microinjected fluorescently labeled nucleotides into replicating DNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by nucleotide incorporation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Some nuclei in the distal tip of the P. pacificus gonad preferentially incorporate fluorescence into the X-chromosomes, which are silenced in the germline, as in C. elegans.
source: The injected nucleotides label nuclei at various stages of S-phase; some preferentially incorporate fluorescence into the X-chromosomes, which are silenced in the germline, as in C. elegans (Kelly et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on nucleotide incorporation data and comparison to C. elegans data from Kelly et al., 2002.

claim: The onset of meiotic prophase in P. pacificus is marked by an obvious change in nuclear organization in which fluorescently stained chromosomes form a conspicuous crescent-shaped mass.
source: The onset of meiotic prophase is marked by an obvious change in nuclear organization in which fluorescently stained chromosomes form a conspicuous crescent-shaped mass (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on cytological observations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Immediately proximal to the 'transition zone' in P. pacificus, DAPI staining reveals parallel tracks, indicative of paired and synapsed homologous chromosomes at the pachytene stage.
source: Immediately proximal to this 'transition zone,' DAPI staining reveals parallel tracks, indicative of paired and synapsed homologous chromosomes at the pachytene stage.
evidence: The claim is based on cytological observations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Gametogenesis switches from spermatogenesis to oogenesis during early adulthood in P. pacificus.
source: Gametogenesis switches from spermatogenesis to oogenesis during early adulthood.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. pacificus development.

claim: As oocytes approach maturation in P. pacificus, chromosomes undergo striking decondensation between diplotene and diakinesis, a stage referred to as the 'growth zone' or 'diffuse stage'.
source: As oocytes approach maturation, chromosomes undergo striking decondensation between diplotene and diakinesis, a stage that has been referred to as the 'growth zone' (Rudel et al., 2005). Similar chromosome morphology is observed during a late 'diffuse stage' of meiotic prophase in many other eukaryotes (Zickler and Kleckner, 1999), but is rarely seen in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rudel et al., 2005 and Zickler and Kleckner, 1999.

claim: Similar chromosome morphology to the 'diffuse stage' is observed during a late stage of meiotic prophase in many other eukaryotes, but is rarely seen in C. elegans.
source: Similar chromosome morphology is observed during a late 'diffuse stage' of meiotic prophase in many other eukaryotes (Zickler and Kleckner, 1999), but is rarely seen in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zickler and Kleckner, 1999.

claim: In the most proximal region of the P. pacificus hermaphrodite gonad, oocytes mature and form a single row of large cells, and chromosomes condense dramatically as the nuclei grow in size.
source: In the most proximal region of the hermaphrodite gonad, oocytes mature and form a single row of large cells, and chromosomes condense dramatically as the nuclei grow in size.
evidence: This is based on cytological observations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Six bivalents can be detected as compact DAPI-staining bodies in P. pacificus oocytes at diakinesis.
source: Six bivalents can be detected as compact DAPI-staining bodies in oocytes at diakinesis, the last stage of meiotic prophase preceding the first meiotic division (Figure 1A and C, Rudel et al., 2005; Sommer et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytological data shown in Figure 1A and C, and citations to Rudel et al., 2005 and Sommer et al., 1996.
